items.prompt: What's the relationship between a Docker image and a Docker container?
choices: They're the same underlying thing — image and container are just two different names for one artifact
An image is a built, immutable artifact (a stack of layers); a container is a running instance of it — like a program file versus a running process
A container is built first from scratch, and an image is only created afterward from that container
An image can only ever produce a single container; running it again requires rebuilding the image first
items.explanation: This is the foundational distinction: `docker build` produces an image once; `docker run` can start many independent containers from that same unchanged image, each with its own running process and writable layer on top.
items.reference:
📦 Image

built once, immutable

▶️ Container

a running instance

Why: the same image can produce many independent containers.
items.learnMore:
Image vs. container

An image is a fixed, content-addressed artifact — a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata. A container is what you get when you actually run it.

ImageContainer
Created bydocker builddocker run
Mutable?NoYes — its own writable layer on top
How many from one image?N/AUnlimited, independent instances

Common mistake

Treating "rebuild the image" and "restart the container" as the same operation. Restarting a container just starts a fresh instance from the same unchanged image; nothing about the image itself is re-derived.

items.prompt: You run `docker run myapp` three times in a row without rebuilding. What do you get?
choices: An error — Docker refuses to run the same image a second time without rebuilding it first
Three independent containers, each a separate running instance of the exact same unchanged image
The same single container being stopped and restarted three separate times in a row
Three brand-new images, one freshly built for each separate run command
items.explanation: `docker run` starts a new container instance every time it's invoked — the image itself is never modified or consumed by running it, so the same image can back any number of simultaneous, independent containers.

built once, immutable

▶️ Container

a running instance

Why: the same image can produce many independent containers.

items.prompt: A container writes a temporary file, then the container is removed. Is that file part of the image now?
choices: Yes, images are automatically updated by anything a running container happens to write
No — a container's writable layer is separate from the image it started from; removing the container discards that layer, leaving the image unchanged
Only if the file was specifically written to the /tmp directory inside the container
Only if the container happened to be running as the root user at the time
items.explanation: The image is immutable by design. A running container gets its own writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers — anything written there lives and dies with that specific container, never touching the image itself.

items.prompt: Why do containers typically start in milliseconds-to-seconds, while a VM takes tens of seconds to minutes?
choices: Containers are always smaller in disk size than any equivalent VM image would be
Containers share the host machine's kernel; a VM has to boot an entire separate guest operating system, kernel included, before anything can run
Containers don't actually start a real process, so there's nothing for them to boot at all
VMs always run on physically slower hardware than the containers they're compared to
items.explanation: The speed gap traces to what each has to bring up: a container reuses the host's already-running kernel, so starting one is closer to starting a process than booting a machine — a VM genuinely has to boot a full guest OS first.
items.reference:
🖥️ VM

own guest OS + kernel, boots fully

📦 Container

shares host kernel, starts like a process

Trade-off: faster, lighter — at a narrower isolation boundary.
items.learnMore:
Containers vs. virtual machines

Both isolate an app from the host, but at different layers of the stack — and that's a trade-off, not a strict improvement in either direction.

VMContainer
KernelOwn guest kernelShares host kernel
Startup timeTens of seconds to minutesMilliseconds to seconds
Isolation boundaryDeeper (full OS)Narrower (shared kernel)

Common mistake

Treating containers as "just lightweight VMs." The mechanism is fundamentally different — sharing a kernel is what buys the speed, and it's also exactly what makes the isolation boundary narrower.

items.prompt: What's the actual trade-off a team accepts when choosing containers over VMs for isolation?
choices: There's no real trade-off at all — containers are strictly better along every single dimension
Faster startup and lower overhead, in exchange for a narrower isolation boundary since the host kernel is shared rather than virtualized
Containers are actually more isolated than VMs, but take longer to start up
VMs simply can't run Linux-based workloads at all, only Windows ones
items.explanation: Sharing the host kernel is exactly what makes containers fast and light — and exactly what makes their isolation boundary narrower than a VM's, which virtualizes a whole separate OS. It's a genuine trade-off, not a flaw in containers.

items.prompt: Does a container include its own kernel, the way a VM includes a guest OS with its own kernel?
choices: Yes, every single container boots and runs its own full kernel at startup time
No — a container has its own filesystem layers and process space, but runs on top of the host machine's existing kernel rather than bringing its own
Only Windows-based containers ever bundle a kernel of their own; Linux ones never do
Only if the Dockerfile explicitly includes a dedicated instruction to install one
items.explanation: A container packages an application and its filesystem, not an operating system kernel — it relies on the host's kernel for process scheduling, memory management, and so on, which is the core mechanical difference from a VM.

items.prompt: What does a registry (like Docker Hub or a private registry) actually let a team do?
choices: Run containers directly on its own, without ever needing a local docker run command
Store and retrieve built images by name and tag — pushing publishes an image, pulling retrieves it, letting one CI build be reused across environments
Automatically rebuild an image from source whenever the underlying code changes
Replace the need for a Dockerfile entirely once an image has been pushed
items.explanation: A registry is purely storage-and-retrieval for images. The actual build-once, run-everywhere guarantee comes from CI pushing exactly one built image and every environment pulling that same one — the registry is the handoff point that makes that possible.
items.reference: CI builds once → pushes to registry → every environment pulls the identical image — not a rebuilt approximation.
items.learnMore:
What a registry is for

A content-addressable store for images, keyed by name and tag and, underneath, by content digest.

ActionWhat happens
docker pushUploads layers the registry doesn't already have
docker pullDownloads layers the local machine doesn't already have

Common mistake

Assuming every environment rebuilds the image from the same Dockerfile. That reintroduces exactly the parity gap Docker exists to close — a rebuild can drift (different base image patch, different dependency resolution) even from identical source.

items.prompt: Why does having CI push one built image to a registry (instead of each environment rebuilding it) matter for environment parity?
choices: It doesn't matter at all — rebuilding from the same Dockerfile always produces identical results
Because every environment pulling the same tag/digest gets the byte-identical artifact CI already tested, not a separately-built approximation
It only really matters for saving disk space across environments, nothing else
Registries are simply required by Docker's license terms to run any image
items.explanation: A rebuild, even from unchanged source, can drift — a different base image patch version, a different dependency resolution at install time. Pulling the exact image CI already built and tested removes that whole class of drift.
items.reference: CI builds once → pushes to registry → every environment pulls the identical image — not a rebuilt approximation.

items.prompt: What produces a new layer in a Docker image?
choices: Each character typed in the Dockerfile
Each instruction in the Dockerfile (FROM, COPY, RUN, etc.) produces its own layer in the resulting image
Layers are created only when the image is pushed to a registry
A single layer holds the entire image; Dockerfiles don't actually produce multiple layers
items.explanation: An image is a stack of layers, one per Dockerfile instruction. That's what makes per-instruction caching possible at all — each layer is independently cacheable because it corresponds to exactly one instruction's effect.
items.reference:
FROM ... ← layer 1
COPY ... ← layer 2
RUN ... ← layer 3

Why: one instruction, one layer, one cache key.
items.learnMore:
Layers, one per instruction

Each layer is cached by a hash of its inputs: the previous layer plus the instruction itself, plus any files it copies in.

InstructionLayer depends on
FROMThe base image tag
COPY x yx's content + previous layer
RUN cmdPrevious layer's output + the command text

Common mistake

Thinking layer order is purely stylistic. It directly determines cache reuse — see L2's cache-invalidation cascade.

items.prompt: A Dockerfile has 6 instructions. Roughly how many layers does the resulting image have?
choices: Always exactly 1, regardless of instruction count
Around 6 — one per instruction, each independently cacheable
It depends only on the image's total file size, not the instruction count
Layers only exist for RUN instructions, not FROM or COPY
items.explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction produces its own layer (FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN — all of them), which is exactly what makes per-layer caching possible: Docker can reuse any layer whose own inputs are unchanged, without touching the rest.
items.reference:
FROM ... ← layer 1
COPY ... ← layer 2
RUN ... ← layer 3

Why: one instruction, one layer, one cache key.

items.prompt: What is a layer's cache key based on?
choices: A random value that gets freshly generated on every single build run
A hash of that layer's actual inputs — the previous layer's output, the instruction itself, and the content of any files it copies in
The current date and time at the moment the build happens to run
The name of the developer who most recently edited the Dockerfile
items.explanation: Content-based hashing is what makes the cache correct, not just fast: a layer only reuses its cached result when its actual inputs are provably unchanged, never based on something incidental like a timestamp.

items.prompt: What's the purpose of a multi-stage Dockerfile build?
choices: It is purely a stylistic convention with no real functional effect on the image at all
One stage uses a full build toolchain (compilers, dev dependencies); a second produces the final image with only what is needed to run
It allows a single Dockerfile to build entirely separate images for several different unrelated applications
It is required by Docker itself whenever a Dockerfile has more than five total instructions
items.explanation: Multi-stage builds separate 'what's needed to build' from 'what's needed to run' — only files explicitly pulled across with COPY --from=<stage> make it into the final image, so compilers and dev tooling from the build stage never ship in production.
items.reference:
Build stage

compiler, dev deps, raw source

Runtime stage

only what COPY --from pulled across
items.learnMore:
Why split build from runtime

A compiler or dev tool sitting in a production image is one more thing that could be exploited if the container is ever compromised, for zero runtime benefit — multi-stage builds remove that for free.

BenefitWhy
Smaller imageLess to pull, less disk
Smaller attack surfaceNo compiler/dev tooling shipped to production

Common mistake

Assuming multi-stage is only about image size. The attack-surface reduction matters just as much, and is easy to overlook.

items.prompt: A Dockerfile compiles TypeScript in one stage and copies only the compiled `dist/` output into a second, final stage. Why not just ship the single-stage version that has everything?
choices: There's no real reason at all — both approaches produce equally sized, equally secure images
The single-stage image would carry the TypeScript compiler and dev dependencies into production, adding size and attack surface for no runtime benefit
Single-stage Dockerfiles technically cannot use the COPY instruction at all
TypeScript specifically cannot ever be compiled without a multi-stage Dockerfile setup
items.explanation: The compiled output is all the running app needs — the compiler and dev dependencies that produced it serve no purpose once compilation is done, but a single-stage build would ship them anyway.
items.reference:

Runtime stage

only what COPY --from pulled across

items.prompt: A Dockerfile has layers in order: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY manifest, RUN npm ci, COPY source. If `package.json` changes, which layers must rebuild?
choices: Only the COPY manifest layer gets rebuilt — every layer after it still reuses its cache
COPY manifest, RUN npm ci, and COPY source — the change cascades to every layer after the one whose inputs changed, since each depends on the one before
Every single layer gets rebuilt, including the FROM and WORKDIR layers at the top
None at all — a package.json change doesn't actually affect the Docker build cache
items.explanation: Invalidation cascades forward, never backward: the manifest layer's cache key changes directly, and every layer after it depends on that layer's output, so npm ci and the final source copy both rebuild too — layers 1 and 2 (FROM, WORKDIR) are untouched since nothing about their own inputs changed.
items.reference:
FROM cached
WORKDIR cached
COPY manifest rebuild
RUN npm ci rebuild (cascade)
COPY source rebuild (cascade)
items.learnMore:
Cascading invalidation

A layer rebuilds if its own inputs changed, OR if any earlier layer it depends on already rebuilt — the cascade only moves forward through the Dockerfile, never backward.

Changed inputLayers that rebuild
source-tree onlyJust the final COPY layer
package.jsonManifest copy → install → source copy

Common mistake

Assuming only the exact layer that copies a changed file rebuilds. Everything after it in the Dockerfile rebuilds too, since each layer's cache key includes the output of the one before it.

items.prompt: In the same 5-layer Dockerfile, only `server.js` (part of the final `COPY . .`) changes — `package.json` doesn't. Which layers rebuild?
choices: All five layers get rebuilt, since Docker always rebuilds top to bottom regardless of what changed
Only the final COPY layer — everything before it (base image, workdir, manifest copy, npm ci) has unchanged inputs and reuses its cache
Only the npm ci layer gets rebuilt; everything else keeps its existing cache
None of the five layers — source file changes never trigger any rebuild
items.explanation: The cascade only starts at the layer whose own inputs actually changed. Since server.js is part of the source tree copied by the final COPY, only that layer's cache key changes — everything before it in the Dockerfile is untouched.
items.reference:
FROM cached
WORKDIR cached
COPY manifest rebuild
RUN npm ci rebuild (cascade)
COPY source rebuild (cascade)

items.prompt: Can invalidation ever cascade backward — a later layer changing causing an earlier layer to rebuild?
choices: Yes, but only whenever that later layer happens to be large enough in size
No — a layer's cache key depends only on its own inputs and the layers before it, never layers after it, so invalidation only moves forward
Yes, but that's only true for RUN instructions specifically, not others
It depends entirely on which specific version of Docker is currently in use
items.explanation: Each layer's cache key is a function of the layer before it plus its own inputs — there's no dependency in the other direction, so a later instruction changing can never invalidate something earlier in the Dockerfile.

WORKDIR cached
COPY manifest rebuild
RUN npm ci rebuild (cascade)
COPY source rebuild (cascade)

items.prompt: Why is it a well-known best practice to COPY dependency manifests and run the install BEFORE copying the rest of the source code?
choices: It has no real effect at all on anything — the order of the COPY instructions is purely cosmetic
It maximizes reuse of the expensive install layer — a source-only change invalidates just the final COPY layer, not the install step
Docker actually requires manifests to be copied before source, or the whole build simply fails
It only ever makes the final image smaller overall, regardless of any caching benefit gained
items.explanation: Putting COPY . . before the install would make the install layer's cache key depend on the entire source tree, invalidating it on every source change — installing first (from just the manifest files) keeps that expensive step cached across ordinary source edits.
items.reference:
COPY . . first

every source edit reruns install

Manifest + install first

source edits skip install entirely
items.learnMore:
Why instruction order has real performance consequences

Ordering doesn't change what the image contains — it changes what depends on what, which is exactly what determines cache reuse.

OrderSource-only edit cost
Manifest → install → sourceFast — install stays cached
Source (all) → installSlow — install reruns every time

Common mistake

Treating this as a micro-optimization. On active development, this ordering is the difference between a multi-second and a near-instant rebuild on every single edit.

items.prompt: A teammate writes `COPY . .` immediately after `FROM`, then installs dependencies afterward. What's the practical consequence during active development?
choices: None at all — Docker is smart enough to skip the install step regardless of instruction order
Every single source edit, even one unrelated to dependencies, invalidates the install layer's cache key, forcing a full reinstall on every rebuild
The image simply fails to build whenever source code changes unrelated to dependencies
It only ever matters the very first time the image gets built, never on any rebuild
items.explanation: Once COPY . . runs before the install, the install layer's cache key includes the entire source tree's content — any source edit changes that key, and the expensive install step reruns even though nothing about the actual dependencies changed.
items.reference:
COPY . . first

every source edit reruns install

Manifest + install first

source edits skip install entirely

items.prompt: You're adding a `RUN apt-get install -y libvips` step (a native OS dependency, unrelated to npm packages) to a Dockerfile. Where should it go to maximize cache reuse?
choices: Immediately after FROM, before anything depending on application files — its key only depends on the base image
After COPY . ., so the install step always has access to the very latest source code
It doesn't matter at all where the OS-level installs go, since they are never cached anyway
Right before CMD, placed at the very end of the entire Dockerfile, after everything else
items.explanation: A step whose real inputs are just the base image (not application source or manifests) should be placed as early as possible — its cache key then depends on nothing that changes often, so it survives both source edits and dependency-manifest edits untouched.

items.prompt: A registry stores and retrieves images "by name and tag, and more precisely, by content digest." What does the content digest actually buy over the tag alone?
choices: Nothing extra at all — a tag and a digest are really just two names for the same guarantee
A digest is derived from the image's content, so it identifies one exact set of bytes; a tag is a movable pointer that can be repointed over time
Digests are only ever used for compressing image layers, not for identifying them
A digest is assigned manually by whoever pushes the image, the same way a tag is
items.explanation: A digest is content-addressed — it can only refer to the exact bytes it was computed from. A tag is a separate, mutable label that a registry maps to whatever image was most recently pushed under that name, which is exactly why tags alone (`latest` especially) don't guarantee reproducibility.
items.reference:
Tag: myapp:1.4.2 — a movable label
Digest: sha256:9f2c... — the exact bytes, always
items.learnMore:
Tags vs. digests

A registry is content-addressable underneath its tag-based interface — pushing/pulling by tag is convenient, but the digest is the actual guarantee.

TagDigest
Mutable?Yes — can be repointedNo — derived from content
Guarantees"Whatever was last pushed here"These exact bytes, always

Common mistake

Treating a version tag as an equally strong guarantee as a digest. A specific tag like 1.4.2 is far more stable in practice than latest, but only a digest is truly immutable.

items.prompt: When `docker pull` retrieves an image, why does it typically only download some layers rather than the entire image?
choices: Registries always send the full image every time; the client just shows a partial progress bar
Layers are individually cached and shared — pulling downloads only the layers the local machine doesn't already have, since each is content-addressed
Docker randomly deletes half the layers locally just to save on bandwidth
Only the base image layer is ever actually transferred; every other layer gets generated locally
items.explanation: Because layers are content-addressed independently of any one image, a machine that already has a given base-image layer cached (from a previous pull of any image sharing that layer) doesn't need to download it again — pulling only fetches what's actually missing locally.
items.reference:

Digest: sha256:9f2c... — the exact bytes, always

items.prompt: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, `npm run build` in the build stage produces `/app/dist`. Does the runtime stage automatically have access to `/app/dist`?
choices: Yes — all stages in a single Dockerfile share the exact same filesystem state by default
No — each stage starts completely fresh; /app/dist only exists in the runtime stage if a COPY --from=build instruction pulls it across
Yes, but only in the specific case where both stages happen to use the same base image
No, and there is actually no way at all to move any files between separate stages
items.explanation: Stage isolation is total by default — nothing from stage 1's filesystem carries over automatically. `COPY --from=<stage>` is the one explicit mechanism for crossing that boundary, and it's opt-in per file/directory, not automatic.
items.reference:
Stage 1 (build): compiler, dev deps, /app/dist
Stage 2 (runtime): starts empty — gets only what COPY --from=build names
items.learnMore:
Stage isolation is the whole mechanism

Isolation between stages is what makes multi-stage builds useful at all — without it, there'd be no way to exclude build tooling from the final image.

What crosses stagesHow
Files/directoriesCOPY --from=<stage> only
Environment variables, installed packagesNever automatically

Common mistake

Assuming a package installed or a variable set in an earlier stage carries forward. It produces confusing "why isn't this here" failures in the final image.

items.prompt: A build stage sets an environment variable with `ENV NODE_ENV=development` to install dev dependencies. Is that variable set in the runtime stage too?
choices: Yes, environment variables always carry across every single stage in a Dockerfile automatically
No — environment variables, like everything else, are stage-local; the runtime stage needs its own ENV instruction if it needs one at all
Only if both stages happen to share the exact same base image tag
Only for variables whose name happens to start with the prefix NODE_
items.explanation: Nothing about a stage's environment is shared automatically — variables, installed packages, and files all stay local to the stage that set them unless explicitly copied across with COPY --from, which doesn't even apply to environment variables (only files).

It is exactly what makes it possible to exclude build-only tooling from the final shipped image entirely
Isolation only really matters for security compliance reasons, never for final image size
Stages are isolated from each other only when using Docker's free tier, not the paid one
items.explanation: The entire value proposition of multi-stage builds depends on stages NOT sharing state by default — that's what guarantees the final image only contains what was explicitly pulled across, rather than everything the build process touched.

items.prompt: CI builds an image once, pushes it to a registry, and staging, QA, and production all pull that same tag. What guarantee does this actually provide that separately rebuilding in each environment wouldn't?
choices: There is no real guarantee at all — pulling an already-built image and rebuilding it are functionally identical
Every environment runs the byte-identical artifact CI already built and tested, closing the drift gap a separate rebuild could open
It only really saves a few CI minutes, with no actual correctness benefit gained at all
It guarantees the deployed application will have exactly zero bugs once it reaches production
items.explanation: The registry is what turns 'built once' into 'run everywhere, identically' — a separate rebuild per environment reintroduces exactly the kind of environment-to-environment drift Docker exists to eliminate, even when the Dockerfile and source are unchanged.
items.reference: CI builds once → push → staging/QA/prod all pull the same digest — never rebuild separately.
items.learnMore:
Build once, run everywhere

This is the practical payoff the rest of the unit's mechanics (layers, caching, registries) exist to serve — not an abstract goal, a specific pipeline shape.

ApproachRisk
Build once, pull everywhereNone — identical bytes everywhere
Rebuild per environmentDrift: base image patch, dependency resolution can differ silently

Common mistake

Assuming "same Dockerfile, same source" is enough for parity. A rebuild can still resolve a different dependency version or pull a different base image patch than the original build did.

items.prompt: Which single mechanic from this unit is most directly responsible for closing L1's opening gap — a laptop passing tests while prod, on different Node/library versions, crashes?
choices: Layer caching specifically, since that is what speeds up local rebuilds the most for developers
The image being a fixed, portable artifact pulled identically everywhere via a registry, not rebuilt per machine
Multi-stage builds specifically, since those only ever affect the build-time tooling involved
The specific choice of base image tag used has no real bearing on this guarantee at all
items.explanation: Layer caching and multi-stage builds are about build speed and image size — the actual environment-parity fix is that the image itself carries every dependency the laptop had, and a registry lets every environment pull that identical artifact instead of reconstructing its own approximation.

items.prompt: Implement `computeRebuildPlan(layers, changedInputs)` from L3: `layers` is an array of `{ name, inputs }` in Dockerfile order; `changedInputs` is a Set of input names that changed. A layer rebuilds if its own inputs changed, OR if any earlier layer already needed a rebuild (invalidation cascades forward). Return an array of the names of every layer that must rebuild, in order.

tests.description: only the last layer rebuilds when only its own input changed
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'A', inputs: ['x'] }, { name: 'B', inputs: ['y'] }], new Set(['y']))).toEqual(['B'])

tests.description: an early layer change cascades to every layer after it
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'A', inputs: ['x'] }, { name: 'B', inputs: ['y'] }, { name: 'C', inputs: [] }], new Set(['x']))).toEqual(['A', 'B', 'C'])

tests.description: no changed inputs means no rebuilds at all
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'A', inputs: ['x'] }, { name: 'B', inputs: ['y'] }], new Set())).toEqual([])

tests.description: a layer with no inputs of its own still rebuilds if cascading from an earlier layer
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'A', inputs: ['x'] }, { name: 'B', inputs: [] }], new Set(['x']))).toEqual(['A', 'B'])

items.explanation: This is the exact rule behind the three real docker build outputs in L3: invalidation only cascades forward — a layer that hasn't changed and follows only unchanged layers stays cached, but once any layer rebuilds, every layer after it must too, since each layer's cache key depends on the output of the one before it.
items.reference:
cascading = false
for each layer: if own-inputs-changed OR cascading → rebuild, cascading = true

Why: a boolean flag is enough because the cascade only ever moves forward.
items.learnMore:
Modeling cache invalidation as a pure function

The real Docker build engine does something equivalent to this, layer by layer, using content hashes instead of a named-input Set — but the logic is the same shape: once a rebuild is triggered, it never un-triggers for the rest of the chain.

This is why a single boolean cascading flag is sufficient — there's no need to track which specific earlier layer triggered the rebuild, only whether the chain has already been broken.

Common mistake

Checking each layer's inputs against the ORIGINAL changedInputs set only, forgetting the cascade — that would incorrectly report a downstream layer as cached even though an earlier layer it depends on already rebuilt.

items.prompt: Implement `computeRebuildPlan(layers, changedInputs)`, same contract as before: `layers` is `[{ name, inputs }]` in order, `changedInputs` is a Set. Return the names of every layer that rebuilds, given that invalidation cascades forward once triggered. Verify it against a 4-layer Dockerfile-shaped chain, including a middle layer with no inputs of its own.

tests.description: a middle layer with no inputs stays cached if nothing before it changed
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'FROM', inputs: ['base'] }, { name: 'WORKDIR', inputs: [] }, { name: 'COPY manifest', inputs: ['pkg'] }, { name: 'RUN install', inputs: [] }], new Set(['pkg']))).toEqual(['COPY manifest', 'RUN install'])

tests.description: changing the base image cascades through the entire chain
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'FROM', inputs: ['base'] }, { name: 'WORKDIR', inputs: [] }, { name: 'COPY manifest', inputs: ['pkg'] }, { name: 'RUN install', inputs: [] }], new Set(['base']))).toEqual(['FROM', 'WORKDIR', 'COPY manifest', 'RUN install'])

tests.description: an unrelated changed input that no layer declares triggers nothing
tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'FROM', inputs: ['base'] }, { name: 'WORKDIR', inputs: [] }], new Set(['unrelated-file']))).toEqual([])

items.explanation: Same rule as before, checked against a shape closer to a real Dockerfile: WORKDIR has no inputs of its own and stays cached when nothing upstream of it changed, but a base-image change (the earliest possible layer) cascades through literally everything after it, since every later layer transitively depends on it.

items.prompt: Implement `shouldIgnore(filePath, patterns)`, a simplified `.dockerignore` matcher. `patterns` is an array of strings like `'node_modules/'` (matches the path or anything inside it) or `'*.log'` (matches any file ending in that suffix, anywhere). Return true if any pattern matches `filePath`.

tests.description: a directory pattern matches files inside that directory
a directory pattern matches the directory path itself
a wildcard suffix pattern matches a file with that extension anywhere
a file not matching any pattern is not ignored
a file that merely contains the pattern text as a substring, not a path/suffix match, is not ignored

items.explanation: A directory pattern ('node_modules/') has to match either the directory itself or anything with that prefix — a plain substring check would wrongly flag unrelated files like 'node_modules_backup.js' that merely contain the same text without actually being inside that directory, which is exactly why the prefix check (not includes()) matters here.
items.reference:
.dockerignore:
node_modules/
.git/
*.log

Why: without it, every build sends and hashes files the app never uses.
items.learnMore:
Why .dockerignore matters beyond just size

Every file in the build context gets sent to the Docker daemon and, for anything a COPY instruction touches, folded into that layer's cache key. Irrelevant files (node_modules, .git, log files) don't just waste bandwidth — they can bloat or destabilize the cache key of a COPY . . layer with content that has nothing to do with the actual application.

Common mistake

Using a naive substring/includes() match for directory patterns. It over-matches unrelated files that merely share a name fragment, which is a correctness bug, not just an inefficiency.

items.prompt: Implement `shouldIgnore(filePath, patterns)` again, this time verified against a mixed set of directory and wildcard patterns applied to a realistic file list, to confirm files that should ship (like `src/server.js`) are never accidentally excluded.

tests.description: a real source file is never ignored by an unrelated pattern set
an exact filename pattern (no wildcard, no trailing slash) matches only that exact path
an exact filename pattern does not match a differently-named file

items.explanation: The exact-match branch (no trailing slash, no wildcard) has to compare full equality, not a prefix or substring — '.env' and '.env.example' are different files, and a pattern meant to exclude only the real secrets file shouldn't accidentally also exclude a checked-in example file with a similar name.
items.reference:
.dockerignore:
node_modules/
.git/
*.log

Why: without it, every build sends and hashes files the app never uses.

items.prompt: Why is pulling an image tagged `latest` risky for reproducible builds, per L3's failure modes?
choices: `latest` images are always corrupted the moment they get pushed to a registry
`latest` is just a mutable tag like any other — it can be repointed to different content at any time, undermining the build-once-run-everywhere guarantee
Docker doesn't actually support the `latest` tag at all; it's a common misconception
`latest` only ever works correctly for base images, never for application images
items.explanation: A tag is just a movable pointer to an image, and `latest` is not special in that regard — a specific version tag or content digest is what actually pins a reproducible reference, since tags in general (latest included) can be repointed.
items.reference: myapp:latest today ≠ myapp:latest tomorrow — same name, possibly different bytes.
items.learnMore:
latest is not a version

latest is Docker's default tag when none is specified — it carries no semantic meaning about recency or stability, it's simply whatever was pushed most recently under that name.

ReferenceReproducible?
myapp:latestNo — can change under you
myapp:1.4.2Mostly — depends on team discipline not to overwrite it
myapp@sha256:...Yes — content-addressed, cannot change

Common mistake

Assuming latest means "the newest, most tested version." It only means "whatever was pushed last" — that could even be an accidental or broken push.

items.prompt: Two deploys, a week apart, both run `docker pull myapp:latest && docker run myapp:latest`. Are they guaranteed to run the same image?
choices: Yes, because tags never change once they've been pushed to a registry
No — if anyone pushed a new image under the `latest` tag that week, the second deploy silently runs different bytes despite an identical command
Yes, but only in the case where the Dockerfile itself didn't change
No, because `docker run` always silently rebuilds the image from source first
items.explanation: A tag is a pointer, and `latest` gets repointed on every push that doesn't specify a different tag — the exact same pull-and-run command a week apart can retrieve genuinely different images with no warning.
items.reference: myapp:latest today ≠ myapp:latest tomorrow — same name, possibly different bytes.

items.prompt: What's the most robust way to reference an image if you need a guarantee that you'll always get the exact same bytes?
choices: Tag it `stable` instead of `latest`, since that name sounds more permanent
Reference it by content digest (e.g. myapp@sha256:...), since a digest is derived from the content and can't be repointed the way a tag can
Always rebuild the image from source instead of ever pulling it
Use the shortest possible tag name so it's less likely to be reused
items.explanation: Any tag, no matter what it's named, is ultimately a mutable pointer someone could repoint. A content digest is the one reference that's inherently tied to specific bytes and cannot be reassigned to different content.

items.prompt: In a multi-stage Dockerfile, a package is installed in the build stage. Does it automatically exist in the runtime stage's final image?
choices: Yes — all stages in a Dockerfile automatically share the exact same filesystem state
No — each stage starts completely fresh; nothing from an earlier stage exists in a later one unless explicitly pulled across with COPY --from=<stage>
Yes, but that's only true for npm packages specifically, not other files
No, multi-stage builds don't actually allow copying anything between stages at all
items.explanation: Stages are isolated by design — this is precisely what makes multi-stage builds useful for excluding build-only tooling from the final image, but it also means anything needed in the final stage (like compiled output) must be explicitly named in a COPY --from instruction.
items.reference: Stage isolation + explicit COPY --from is the entire mechanism multi-stage builds rely on.
items.learnMore:
Stage isolation, revisited with real failure examples

The failure mode isn't hypothetical: a runtime image that mysteriously can't find a binary the build stage installed is almost always this exact mistake — the install happened in a stage whose filesystem never crosses into the final image.

Common mistake

Debugging a "missing binary in production" issue by re-checking the build stage's Dockerfile lines, when the real fix is adding a COPY --from for that specific file.

items.prompt: A runtime image mysteriously can't find a compiled binary that the build stage's Dockerfile clearly installs. What's the most likely cause?
choices: The binary was installed in the build stage with the wrong file permissions
The build stage never copied it across with COPY --from=<stage> — it exists only inside the build stage's own isolated filesystem
Docker silently deletes any binary file larger than 10MB during the build
The base images used in the two different stages are incompatible with each other
items.explanation: This is the single most common multi-stage debugging trap: the binary genuinely was installed, just in a stage whose filesystem is completely separate from the final image unless a COPY --from names it explicitly.
items.reference: Stage isolation + explicit COPY --from is the entire mechanism multi-stage builds rely on.

items.prompt: Fixing a "binary not found in production" bug caused by multi-stage isolation requires which change?
choices: Switching back to a single-stage Dockerfile permanently instead of a multi-stage one
Adding an explicit COPY --from=<build-stage-name> <path> instruction in the runtime stage naming that specific file or directory
Increasing the runtime stage's memory limit so the file fits during the copy
Rebuilding the entire build stage a second time inside the runtime stage itself
items.explanation: The fix is narrow and explicit: name exactly what needs to cross the stage boundary with COPY --from. Going back to single-stage would fix the symptom but throw away every benefit (image size, attack surface) multi-stage builds provide.

items.prompt: A `RUN apt-get install -y libvips` step (a native OS dependency) only ever depends on the base image, never on application source or package.json. Where does it survive the most cache invalidation if placed there?
choices: Right before CMD, placed at the very end of the entire Dockerfile's instructions
As early as possible, right after FROM — its cache key then depends on nothing that changes on ordinary source or manifest edits
It has to go after COPY package.json, or Docker will reject the whole Dockerfile
Placement makes no real difference at all for OS-level install steps specifically
items.explanation: The general rule extends past npm installs: any step whose real inputs are limited to the base image should sit as early as possible, since that minimizes what could invalidate it — it then survives both source edits and manifest edits, only rebuilding if the base image itself changes.
items.reference: General rule: place a layer as early as its real inputs allow — not just dependency installs, anything genuinely base-image-only.
items.learnMore:
Layer ordering generalizes past npm ci

The dependency-manifest-before-source pattern is one instance of a broader rule: order layers by how often their actual inputs change, cheapest/most-stable first. An OS-level package install that never depends on application files is exactly this case.

Common mistake

Only applying the "install before source" rule to npm/pip-style installs, and missing that the same reasoning applies to any layer with genuinely stable inputs.

items.prompt: What's the general principle behind "copy manifests and install dependencies before copying source," once you generalize it past that one specific case?
choices: Every RUN instruction should always come before every COPY instruction, with no exceptions
Order layers by how often their inputs actually change — the most stable steps as early as possible, so they survive the widest range of edits
Instruction order is purely a style preference with no measurable effect on builds
Only steps that involve a package manager actually benefit from being placed early
items.explanation: The npm-ci-before-source pattern is a specific case of a general rule: put whatever changes least often earliest, so the most expensive, most stable steps get invalidated the least frequently.
items.reference: General rule: place a layer as early as its real inputs allow — not just dependency installs, anything genuinely base-image-only.
